newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk prosecutor charged over TV comments.
newsitem.headline: Turk prosecutor charged over TV comments.

text.p: A Turkish high court has charged a senior prosecutor for his comments on a current affairs television programme that the country's judiciary was not independent of politics, television said.

Private ATV television said late on Monday that state security court prosecutor Mete Gokturk was to be tried at the high court of appeals for insulting the judiciary and justice ministry in ATV's weekly "Political Arena" debate programme.
The charges carry a jail sentence of up to 12 years. Court officials were not immediately available for comment.

In the programme, broadcast in November, Gokturk said there were many problems with the judiciary, including inappropriate and dated punishments, but that with the present composition of parliament there would be no headway against the problems.

"I believe the judiciary is not independent in Turkey. In a country where the judiciary is not free, you cannot have a democracy," Gokturk said. "Constitutional articles restricting the independence of the judiciary must be changed."

The present constitution was created in 1982 by the military in charge following a coup in 1980. The state security courts -- which have jailed scores of writers and intellectuals for writings and speeches under much-critised laws restricting expression -- where created during an earlier military era.
Human rights groups regularly criticise Turkish courts, especially the state security courts, for not being independent.
Gokturk found an ally in a senior prosecutor from the high court of appeals where he is to be tried.

"(In the 1980 coup) the independence of the judiciary in Turkey was hit hard," prosecutor Sami Selcuk told ATV, defending the right of prosecutors to speak out. "It is not possible for such a country to enter the world stage with big ambitions."
Turkey's European allies have cited widespread human rights problems and an unjust legal system as main factors preventing Ankara's long-standing goal of joining the European Union.
Selcuk said the problems of the judiciary were discussed every year by prosecutors and judges but he said politicians of all colours always ended up by blocking attempts at autonomy.

The programme was broadcast shortly after a crash in which a top policeman and a wanted gangster died in the same car. A government MP was also in the car but escaped. The crash sparked a controversy over ties between the state and organised crime.
